Kelso
KEL-soh
n. (the Border abbey of the Tironensians, greatest of the four, whose surviving transept served as the parish kirk until 1771)
Old English calc hoh, the chalk or limestone heugh, the spur of rock above the Tweed where the abbey stands.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Kelso is the Border town where the Teviot joins the Tweed, and its abbey was the greatest of the four great houses of the Scottish Borders. The Tironensian community that David I had planted at Selkirk in 1113 was moved there in 1128, and the church they built, with a double transept and a massive west tower, was the largest and richest in the region; the abbot had precedence over all other Scottish abbots and the house held some forty churches. James III was crowned in it in 1460 as a boy of eight. Like Melrose it was destroyed by war rather than by reformers, burned in 1523 and again in 1542, and finally stormed by Hertford's force in 1545, when the defenders, including twelve monks, were killed in the tower. After the Reformation the parish fitted up the surviving western transept as its kirk, built a floor and galleries inside it and worshipped there for two centuries until the structure was condemned in 1771. The dictionary records the transept kirk with approval and states the principle it illustrates.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a transept as the cross aisle of a church; a gallery as a raised floor for spectators; to fit up as to prepare for use; a plummet as a weight for sounding; and small things as matters of little account.

expand to see more

TRANSEPT, n. In architecture, the cross aisle of a church, lying across the nave at right angles.

GALLERY, n. A covered passage; in a church, an elevated floor or platform for the accommodation of hearers.

FIT, v.t. To adapt; to suit; to make suitable; to prepare; to furnish with what is proper.

PLUMMET, n. A long piece of lead attached to a line, used in sounding the depth of water; a plumb line.

SMALL, a. Slender; thin; fine; of little size; minute; of little consequence or importance.

Modern Corruption

Greatest of the four Border abbeys, Tironensian from 1128, where James III was crowned in 1460 and whose defenders were killed in the tower in 1545, its surviving transept serving as the parish kirk until 1771.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a building exists for the congregation that uses it, and that fitting a floor and galleries into the stump of a ruined abbey is a better act than either venerating the ruin or pulling it down for stone. Kelso's parish did the sensible thing for two hundred years. Ezra records the mixed feeling that attends such work honestly, for when the foundation of the second house was laid the old men who had seen the first “wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy” (Ezr 3:12); both reactions were right, and neither stopped the building.

The second thing to recover is Zechariah's rebuke to those who measure a work by its grandeur, which was spoken to men rebuilding a temple that would not match what had stood there: “For who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10). A parish in a transept is a day of small things, and so is almost every genuine recovery. Nehemiah's way of putting the proposal is the pattern for it, a statement of the facts followed immediately by a call to work: “Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17). What the finished thing is for is stated by Habakkuk, and it is not architecture: “But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20). The dictionary notes that the abbot of Kelso once took precedence over every abbot in Scotland, and that the most useful thing the house ever did was to leave a transept big enough to hold a parish.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yesud-sense of foundation in Ezra 3; Hebrew qaton (H6996), small; Hebrew banah (H1129), to build.

expand to see more

Hebrew bakah-sense of weeping in Ezra's account — “wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy”, Ezra 3:12.

Hebrew qaton (H6996) — small, little, insignificant; “who hath despised the day of small things?”, Zechariah 4:10.

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build, to rebuild; “let us build up the wall of Jerusalem”, Nehemiah 2:17.

Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, shame; “that we be no more a reproach”, Nehemiah 2:17.

Hebrew hekal (H1964) — a large building, a temple; “But the LORD is in his holy temple”, Habakkuk 2:20.

Usage

"“wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy” (Ezr 3:12) — a parish in the ruin of the greatest Border abbey."

"“who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10) — galleries fitted into a transept."

"“let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20) — what the finished thing is for."
